title: Sleep and Recovery
summary: Protect a window → Wind down → Ease the day → Review the week
subtitle: Make room for rest so movement fits your real life.

blocks.text: A fitness app may send a cheerful workout reminder at the exact moment you finally sit down. Its calendar has never worked a late shift or settled a child after midnight. Rest deserves space in your plan, even when the reminder has excellent graphics.
Wake up more ready for your day.
blocks.detail: Knowing how much rest you need, and protecting it, makes every other healthy habit easier to keep.
blocks.extra: Section 03 shows you how to build sleep around your real schedule.

blocks.text: Recovery means giving yourself time and support to feel ready again after activity and everyday demands. Sleep is part of recovery, along with breaks and manageable movement. A hard workday counts when you decide how much extra activity fits.

The time you set aside for sleep is your sleep opportunity. The time you’re asleep can be shorter, since falling asleep and waking in the night use some of it. Eight hours between getting into bed and getting up doesn’t mean eight hours of sleep.

Canada’s movement guidelines recommend regular, good-quality sleep: 7 to 9 hours a night for adults aged 18 to 64, and 7 to 8 hours for adults 65 and older, with steady bedtimes and wake-up times. Your work or caregiving schedule may need its own pattern.

This lesson is general learning, not insomnia treatment or a medical plan. Talk to a clinician about sleep trouble that lasts, loud snoring with pauses in breathing, or daytime sleepiness that gets in the way of daily tasks. For long-lasting insomnia, the first treatment doctors usually recommend is a type of coaching called CBT-I, not sleeping pills. Never drive while drowsy.

Start with the responsibilities that shape your sleep window. A shift worker may need to sleep in the day, while a caregiver may have broken nights. Look for a routine you can repeat on similar days, instead of copying someone else’s bedtime.

Make your sleeping space quiet, dark and a comfortable temperature. Choose one change you can afford, like closing a blind or asking others to keep the noise down. You don’t need a new mattress before trying a small fix.
Protect a window, not a score. Write down when sleep could fit before you buy a tracker. A device can’t create time that work and caregiving have already used up.

Give your last tasks a stopping point before bed. For example, put tomorrow’s lunch in the fridge, leave a note for an unfinished chore and move work messages out of reach. Choose a quiet activity that won’t turn into another job.

Caffeine can keep you alert when you want to sleep, and its effects last for hours, so many people stop having it about six hours before bed. Health Canada suggests adults have no more than 400 mg a day, about three small cups of brewed coffee. Alcohol can disrupt sleep even if it makes you sleepy at first. Ask a pharmacist or clinician about medicine concerns instead of changing a prescription yourself.

items.title: “Alcohol is a reliable sleep aid.”
items.text: Feeling sleepy after a drink doesn’t mean your sleep will be restful. Alcohol can make you wake up more during the night.

blocks.text: Recovery belongs in your movement plan too. After a demanding day, choose a shorter familiar activity, an easier version or a rest day instead of adding another hard session. Regular meals and water are part of recovery, no supplements required. For example, pack your usual sandwich and fruit for after a walk after work, and bring water.
Make the easier option specific. “Walk gently for five minutes if it feels comfortable” is a clearer backup than “do something.” Taking a rest day is a valid choice too.

sections.title: Fictional learning story: The curtain note

blocks.text: The curtain note
paragraphs: Mara worked rotating shifts at a food plant in Saskatoon. She wanted enough energy to join her sister’s Saturday walks without spending the afternoon on the couch. Her kitchen calendar had walking dates on it, but no space marked for rest.

After three late shifts in a row, Mara slept through their meeting time. Her sister’s message was kind, but Mara worried their weekly time together would fade away. Before agreeing to another early start, she decided to look at her week.

For seven days, she privately noted the sleep window she planned and how rested she felt when she woke. The problem was clear. Laundry and grocery runs were eating the hours she meant to protect. A longer walk wouldn’t fix that.

Mara could keep the early Saturday walk or ask for a later one. She called her sister and moved the walk to the afternoon. She asked her roommate to leave the laundry until she woke up. After late shifts, she chose a ten-minute easy walk instead of her usual longer route.

The first protected morning still went badly, because sunlight spilled past the bedroom curtain. Her roommate saw the note asking for quiet and pointed out that the curtain had slipped off one hook. Fixing it took two minutes, which beat the new blackout curtains Mara had started pricing.

The next week was mixed, with one surprise shift change. Mara kept two planned sleep windows and joined the shorter Saturday walk. She didn’t pretend every tired day was gone. Beside the next walking date, she wrote “rest window” and drew a tiny curtain hook.

blocks.text: Ask for a clear change. A request like “Could the laundry wait until I wake up on Tuesday?” gives someone an easy way to help.
One small fix can protect a lot of rest.
blocks.detail: A practical change to your schedule or space makes rest easier to keep, without rebuilding your whole life.
blocks.extra: Section 05 gives you a fifteen-minute wind-down and a seven-day review.

blocks.text: Choose one sleep window that fits tomorrow’s duties, then get ready for it. Treat the plan below as an example you can adjust, not a personal prescription. It doesn’t ask you to sleep less or force yourself to sleep on command.
Adjustable 15-minute wind-down example

items.title: Minutes 0–5: finish one needed preparation, such as setting out work clothes
Minutes 5–8: lower room light and put non-urgent messages aside
Minutes 8–15: read something quiet or listen to gentle music
Total: 5 + 3 + 7 = 15 minutes before your planned sleep window

blocks.text: If fifteen minutes doesn’t fit, try five minutes for one helpful step. Keep essential caregiving or emergency contacts within reach. The routine is an invitation to settle down, not a test you fail if you stay awake.
A shorter wind-down is fine on a busy day. It isn’t a reason to cut into the sleep time you’re trying to protect.
Observe for seven days

On days 1 to 3, privately note your planned sleep window, a rough guess at your sleep if it helps and how ready you feel for everyday tasks. On days 4 to 6, try one change, like a darker room. On day 7, review what helped and what still needs support. Repeat the week if it’s useful.

For movement, decide before you start whether today calls for your usual session, an easier option or rest. Low energy is different from pain or injury, which you shouldn’t push through. Stop with new pain, dizziness, chest discomfort or unusual breathlessness, and get appropriate care.
Change one thing at a time. Keeping the rest of your plan the same makes it easier to tell whether the change helps.

items.title: “A missed workout must be added to tomorrow.”
items.text: Doubling the next session can crowd out recovery. Go back to a manageable plan instead.

blocks.text: Insider tip: Keep a simple indoor option for icy paths, extreme cold or smoky summer air. Checking local conditions before an outdoor session saves you getting ready for a route you can’t use.
Quick Check

items.title: Does eight hours in bed prove eight hours asleep?
items.text: Time awake can use part of the sleep opportunity.

items.title: What can you choose after a demanding shift?
items.detail: An easier familiar activity or rest can fit the day.

items.title: Should you drive when you feel drowsy?

blocks.text: Knowledge Check

items.title: Lee has eight hours available for sleep but is awake for part of it. Which is accurate? A. Lee certainly slept eight hours. · B. Sleep opportunity and actual sleep can differ. · C. Lee must exercise longer.
items.text: Time available includes time awake, so it cannot confirm the amount slept.

items.title: Sam finishes a tiring shift before a planned walk. What fits this lesson? A. Double the walking time. · B. Ignore new pain. · C. Choose an easier version or rest.
items.text: Daily demands matter when choosing activity; pain should not be pushed through.

items.title: Jo hears that their partner snores loudly and has breathing pauses. What should Jo suggest? A. Get clinician advice. · B. Diagnose the cause from a tracker. · C. Try alcohol before sleep.
items.text: Breathing pauses need professional advice, and this course cannot identify the cause.

items.title: Write one sleep-support step and a review time that could fit a changing schedule.
items.text: After each late shift, I will close the blind before settling. I will review whether this was workable after seven days.

blocks.text: Protect an achievable sleep opportunity, use a simple routine, and let your movement plan include easier days and rest.
Write your own small recovery plan below. Keep detailed sleep notes and private health information in your own notebook.
Check that your plan names a step you can take, not a result you must achieve.

items.title: Sleep opportunity
items.text: Time you have made available for sleep.

items.title: Actual sleep
items.text: Time spent asleep within that opportunity.

items.title: Wind-down
items.text: A short routine to help you settle before sleep.

items.title: Recovery
items.text: Time and support after activity or daily demands.

items.title: Easier day
items.text: A day with less demanding movement.

items.title: Drowsy
items.text: Sleepy enough that staying alert is difficult.
